item.content:encoded:
The mighty nor’easter that’s expected to rock the East Coast all the weekend threw a curveball to the Yankees, whose game on Saturday night was preemptively rescheduled for Friday as part of a single-admission doubleheader.
Although the Yankees’ final series of the regular season is inconsequential to the standings — they are locked into the American League’s No. 4 seed — the development affected fans who had planned to attend Saturday’s game against the Baltimore Orioles for CC Sabathia’s number retirement ceremony.
The ceremony was rescheduled for Friday before the Yankees and Orioles began their first game of the day at 4:05 p.m. EDT.
Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances and Chris Young were among the alumni attending the No. 52 retirement and Monument Park plaque unveiling at Yankee Stadium, where Sabathia called home for 11 of his 19 MLB seasons.
Sabathia — a culture-setting leader and ace who helped the Yankees win the 2009 World Series — entered the National Baseball Hall of Fame as a first-ballot inductee last year with a Yankees hat on his plaque.
Only tickets dated for Sept. 25 were eligible for Friday’s doubleheader. Tickets dated for Sept. 26 can be exchanged for a “similar regular season game at Yankee Stadium,” the Yankees announced.
As originally planned, the first 18,000 ticketed guests to arrive at the stadium Friday would receive a bobblehead depicting Knicks star Josh Hart in a Yankees jersey. Hart is the great-nephew of former Yankees catcher Elston Howard, whose No. 32 is retired by the team.
Officials warned of heavy rainfall, sustained winds of 25-35 mph and the potential of coastal flooding in New York, with the worst of it expected to occur from Saturday evening into Sunday afternoon.
The Yankees’ regular season finale remains scheduled for Sunday afternoon.
“I don’t worry about things out of my hands,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Thursday night’s 6-4 win against the Tampa Bay Rays. “Saturday’s out of the question. We’ll see what Sunday brings.”
Neither the Yankees nor Orioles have anything left to play for in terms of game results, though canceling Sunday’s game — and thus giving the Yankees a weekend of rest — could provide an inequitable advantage going into the playoffs.
The Yankees are set to begin their Wild Card series in the Bronx on Tuesday night, when the weather looks much clearer.

The New York Yankees will begin a series against the Baltimore Orioles on Friday afternoon with a doubleheader.
Before the first game, the Yankees will retire legendary pitcher CC Sabathia’s number after he spent 11 seasons with the organization from 2009 to 2019. Sabathia made three All-Star teams and posted a 134-88 record with a 3.81 ERA during his Yankees tenure.
Derek Jeter Featured in Yankees’ Announcement
On Friday morning, the Yankees shared some important details about the pregame ceremony surrounding Sabathia’s jersey retirement, which will also feature MLB and Yankees legend Derek Jeter.
They revealed that Jeter will be in attendance alongside Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young.
“Today’s CC Sabathia Ceremony will begin at 3:15 p.m. Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, Dellin Betances, and Chris Young are set to join @CC_Sabathia as we honor his career and legacy,” the Yankees posted on X.
“All @yankeestadium gates will open to fans at 2:30 p.m., at which time distribution will begin for the September 25 scheduled promotional item (Josh Hart Yankees Bobblehead presented by Delta Air Lines for the first 18,000 guests in attendance).”

How Long Were Jeter and Sabathia Teammates?
Jeter has long been a staple of the Yankees franchise after everything he accomplished during his illustrious 20-year career with the organization.
He made his MLB debut in 1995, and 14 years later, he became teammates with Sabathia, who joined the Yankees after already spending nine years in the league.
The two spent six seasons together as teammates from 2009 until Jeter retired after the 2014 season. They won a World Series together in 2009, which was Sabathia’s first and Jeter’s fifth.

item.content:encoded:
There will never be another No. 52 in pinstripes.
On Friday, the Yankees will make official what has felt inevitable for years, retiring CC Sabathia’s number and unveiling a plaque in his honor in Monument Park before New York’s 4:05 p.m. game against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
It is one of the highest honors the franchise can bestow, and for Sabathia, it comes barely a year after baseball gave him its highest honor.
The big left-hander was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2025, making it to Cooperstown on his first ballot. Now No. 52 will hang permanently at Yankee Stadium, ensuring that the number Sabathia wore for all 11 of his seasons in the Bronx belongs to him forever.
Sabathia will become the 24th Yankees player or manager to have his number retired. Because No. 8 is shared by Bill Dickey and Yogi Berra, 52 will become the 23rd different number removed from circulation by the franchise. He is the first Yankee to receive the honor since Paul O’Neill’s No. 21 was retired in 2022.
A Hall of Fame Career That Found a Home in the Bronx
Sabathia’s road to Monument Park began before he ever put on pinstripes.
He debuted with Cleveland as a 20-year-old in 2001, developed into one of baseball’s premier starting pitchers and won the 2007 American League Cy Young Award. After a remarkable second half with Milwaukee in 2008, when he helped carry the Brewers into the postseason, Sabathia became the centerpiece of the Yankees’ aggressive offseason plans.
New York signed him to a seven-year, $161 million contract in December 2008, at the time the largest free-agent contract ever given to a pitcher.
He immediately delivered.
Sabathia went 19-8 with a 3.37 ERA across 34 starts in 2009, anchoring the rotation as the Yankees returned to the World Series. He was even better when October arrived, earning ALCS MVP honors after going 2-0 with a 1.13 ERA against the Angels. Weeks later, the Yankees were World Series champions for the 27th time.
It would be the beginning of an 11-season relationship between Sabathia and New York.
From 2009 through his retirement in 2019, Sabathia went 134-88 with a 3.81 ERA and 1,700 strikeouts as a Yankee. His name remains scattered throughout the franchise’s pitching record book, ranking fourth in Yankees history in strikeouts, seventh in starts, 10th in wins and 11th in innings pitched.
Sabathia was also a fixture when the games mattered most. In 21 postseason appearances for New York, including 18 starts, he went 8-4 with a 3.42 ERA. At Yankee Stadium, his postseason ERA was just 2.17.
Those numbers tell a large part of the story. They do not tell all of it.
Sabathia became one of the defining personalities of his Yankees era, a clubhouse leader whose importance stretched well beyond what happened every fifth day. By the time he threw the final pitch of his career in 2019, he had long since become synonymous with the pinstripes.
First-Ballot Hall of Famer
Baseball made Sabathia’s place among the game’s greats official in January 2025.
In his first year of eligibility, Sabathia received 86.8 percent of the Baseball Writers’ Association of America vote, easily clearing the 75 percent needed for election into the National Baseball Hall of Fame. He was officially inducted in Cooperstown on July 27, 2025.
His complete career resume left little question about his Cooperstown credentials.
Across 19 Major League seasons with Cleveland, Milwaukee and New York, Sabathia finished 251-161 with a 3.74 ERA. He pitched 3,577 1/3 innings, made six All-Star teams, won a Cy Young Award and struck out 3,093 batters.
He also joined one of baseball’s most exclusive pitching clubs.
Sabathia is one of just 15 pitchers in Major League history to record at least 250 victories and 3,000 strikeouts. When he reached those milestones, only fellow Hall of Famers Randy Johnson and Steve Carlton had done both as left-handers.
And when it came time to decide which team would be represented on his Hall of Fame plaque, Sabathia chose the interlocking NY.
Cooperstown may celebrate his entire career, but Sabathia has made clear where he considers home.
Sabathia’s place in baseball history is already secure, but the family name is still very much part of the game. I had the chance to catch up with him during MLB All-Star Week this summer, just days after the Brewers selected his son, Carsten Sabathia III, in the 2026 MLB Draft. Given CC’s own memorable run in Milwaukee, the connection felt especially fitting, and I asked him if watching his son turn pro had him tempted to pull a LeBron-and-Bronny and come out of retirement for one last chance to share the field.
Another Left-Hander Among Yankees Pitching Royalty
Now Sabathia’s legacy will have a permanent home in center field alongside some of the greatest pitchers to ever wear pinstripes.
When Mariano Rivera received his Monument Park plaque in 2016, he became the ninth Yankees pitcher honored there, joining Lefty Gomez, Whitey Ford, Red Ruffing, Allie Reynolds, Ron Guidry, Goose Gossage, Andy Pettitte and Mel Stottlemyre. Sabathia will add another name to that pitching fraternity.
Several members of that group have an additional distinction that Sabathia will now share.
Ford’s No. 16, Rivera’s No. 42, Pettitte’s No. 46 and Guidry’s No. 49 have all been retired by the Yankees. On Friday, Sabathia’s No. 52 joins them.
There is something especially fitting about Sabathia taking his place alongside Pettitte and Rivera.
They were there with him in 2009, when Sabathia arrived in New York carrying enormous expectations and immediately helped deliver a championship. Derek Jeter’s No. 2, Jorge Posada’s No. 20, Rivera’s No. 42 and Pettitte’s No. 46 have all since been retired. Sabathia now becomes the fifth member of that 2009 championship team to receive the same honor.
Seventeen years after that group brought a World Series trophy back to the Bronx, another piece of the 2009 Yankees will become a permanent part of the ballpark.
52 Forever
Sabathia arrived in New York as an ace with a massive contract and expectations to match.
He leaves his mark on the franchise as something much bigger.
World Series champion. ALCS MVP. Clubhouse leader. More than 1,700 strikeouts in pinstripes. First-ballot Hall of Famer.
And now, forever, No. 52.
Future generations of Yankees fans walking through Monument Park will see Sabathia’s plaque among the franchise’s legends. They’ll look beyond the center-field wall and see his number alongside Ford, Rivera, Pettitte, Guidry and the countless icons who came before him.
Players will come and go. Rotations will change. New aces will take the mound in the Bronx.
But no Yankee will wear 52 again.
That one belongs to CC.

item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball’s playoffs are coming soon and Alex Bregman will be a part of it.
Of course he is.
Bregman made baseball history Thursday, Sept. 24 when the Chicago Cubs clinched a National League wild-card berth with a victory over the Miami Marlins. And for the 10th consecutive year, injured eye willing, Bregman will take part in the postseason, this time with a twist.
Bregman, the Cubs’ 32-year-old third baseman, will become the first position player to play postseason baseball 10 consecutive seasons with multiple teams. In fact, he’s done it with three ballclubs – eight straight years with the Houston Astros and then the past two with the Boston Red Sox and Cubs, as he settled for good in Chicago by signing a five-year, $175 million contract in January.
And it seems like wherever Bregman goes, October baseball follows.
Texas loves him anyway
Bregman was a two-time All-Star and two-time champion in Houston, the brash young slugger in his first full season when they won the 2017 World Series, the MVP runner-up when they lost the 2019 Series in seven games.
After bearing much of the scorn for the club’s 2017 sign-stealing scandal, he was the chastened veteran on the 2022 squad that won a second World Series, this time without a cloud of controversy to follow.
Yet Bregman’s chops as a club cornerstone gained greater veracity a year ago, when he left the Astros and, combining his production with his baseball smarts and clubhouse gravitas, lifted the Red Sox to the postseason for the first time in three years as the Astros missed the playoffs for the first time since 2016.
Those vibes were as attractive to the Cubs as Bregman’s career .846 OPS when they pursued him after he opted out of his contract with Boston. And it’s all come together in Wrigleyville: Thanks to a second-half surge, Bregman has hit 26 home runs, posted an .804 OPS and produced 5.4 WAR, second only to presumed MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong on the Cubs.
“Anytime Alex Bregman is playing an Alex Bregman brand of baseball, it’s just good for the program,” Crow-Armstrong told USA TODAY Sports last month.
And if he manages to play just days after suffering a gruesome eye injury, the legend will only grow.
Heroes of the fall
Bregman’s postseason constancy has put himself among some legendary and curious October stalwarts.
Advertisement
Unsurprisingly, the consecutive postseasons list is littered with alumni from the three dominant playoff groups of the wild-card era: The 1990s Atlanta Braves, the late-century New York Yankees and the current batch of Los Angeles Dodgers.
Yankees closer Mariano Rivera tops the list, appearing in 13 consecutive postseasons from 1995-2007, followed by Derek Jeter, whose 12-year streak began a year after Rivera’s playoff debut.
Catcher Jorge Posada and Braves Hall of Famers Chipper Jones and Tom Glavine all played in 11 consecutive postseasons. As did lefty reliever Mike Stanton, who did it with four teams – the Braves, Red Sox, Yankees and Texas Rangers – between 1991-2002.
Who let him in?
Bregman, longtime Dodgers closer Kenley Jansen and Hall of Famer Greg Maddux all reached 10 consecutive postseasons. Current Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman and longtime third baseman Justin Turner are at the nine-year mark, Freddie winning a World Series championship with Atlanta in 2021 and two more in L.A. the past two seasons.
Retired Dodgers lefty Clayton Kershaw leads the “but for” category: He pitched in eight consecutive postseasons from 2013-2020, and would have made it 13 in a row if not for injuries in 2021 and 2024. Same with Braves Hall of Famer John Smoltz – he was present for all of Atlanta’s 14 consecutive division titles yet underwent Tommy John surgery in 2000.
And several likely 2026 participants had streaks broken thanks to one unlucky season – such as slugger Kyle Schwarber, who’d be working on a 12-year streak with the Cubs, Red Sox and Phillies if not for the 2019 Cubs missing the playoffs. Same with Mookie Betts, ticketed for his 10th postseason in 11 years with the Dodgers and Boston, missing only in ’19 with the Red Sox.
The wild-card format – which began in 1995 and expanded in 2012 and 2022 – makes this list unavoidably modern due to the expanded access it affords. Still, some players from past eras were near-constants in the playoffs.
Mr. October himself, Reggie Jackson, reached the postseason 10 times in 12 years from 1971 to 1982, winning four World Series with the Oakland Athletics and New York Yankees, and then, just for kicks, reaching the 1982 ALCS with the California Angels.
The great Yogi Berra was a 10-time World Series champion, but his longest consecutive streak of playoff runs was five years. Yet reaching the World Series 14 times in 17 years, when only two teams reached the playoffs, remains a stunning feat.
So perhaps Bregman - even with 102 career postseason games, 19 homers, 91 hits and a .791 OPS - has a little more work to do to match some of the legends of October. Yet from Houston to Boston to Chicago, he’s leaving little doubt that wherever he goes, winning follows.

This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced.
Yet, as the Yankees look towards Tuesday, when they open the playoffs at home against what is virtually certain to be the Boston Red Sox, their longtime nemesis, in a best-of-three wildcard series, the prospects of them navigating an always perilous path to the World Series were reduced when Yankees manager Aaron Boone said this past Tuesday that the reigning American League MVP likely won’t play in the series due to a right calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone revealed to reporters.
Judge, who has only appeared in 66 games this season, primarily recovering from a right rib stress fracture, which caused him to sit out 84 games from May 31 to Sept. 8, is now on the 10-day injured list, placed there last Friday. The 34-year-old Judge, arguably the best player in the sport over the last decade, isn’t expected back for the divisional round if the Yankees get by the Red Sox.
Last weekend, Boone informed the media the team didn’t have a firm estimate as to when Judge, a three-time AL MVP, three-time AL home run leader, two-time MLB RBI king and last season’s MLB batting champion, would return to the lineup.
“I mean, I have no idea, we’re in the early stages,” expressed Boone, now in his ninth season as the Yankees manager. “We’ll just obviously treat it and see what transpires.”
The Yankees watched Tampa Bay clinch the AL East title on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium when they won the second game of a double-header on Tuesday 6-1. The Yankees shut out the Rays in the opener. Tampa Bay 96-61 going into the third game of the four-game series last night with the finale scheduled for 7:05 tonight. The Yankees were second in the division at 90-67 and the 84-73 Red Sox third.
With Judge unavailable, the Yankees offense will have to be multifaceted — both power and small ball will be required to make a deep postseason run. Designated hitter Ben Rice, who as of Wednesday had 39 home runs and 95 RBIs, both team highs, was the only Yankee with more than 20 homers and 80 runs batted in, so timely power will have to come from sources such as second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (19 home runs), first baseman Paul Goldschmidt (18), and left fielder Cody Bellinger (17).
But it is pitching that must advance the Yankees, led by leading AL Cy Young Award candidate Cam Schlittler, who is 14-6 with a 1.94 ERA and 234 strikeouts. Schlittler is scheduled to start tonight before taking the mound next week in the wildcard series.
But the prevailing question is: Can the Yankees win without Judge?

Ben Rice is in the process of wrapping up a breakout season for the New York Yankees. That included making some history on Wednesday.
Facing the Tampa Bay Rays, the All-Star first baseman opened the scoring in the first inning with his 40th homer of the season. It was a second-deck no-doubter off a first-pitche sinker from Rays starter Mason Englert.
Then he hit another in the fourth inning, putting him in a four-way tie for the AL lead at 41 homers with Pete Alonso, Yordan Álvarez and Junior Caminero.
By reaching 40 homers in a season, Rice has entered rare territory. As MLB.com's Sarah Langs notes, he joins teammate Aaron Judge as the second Yankees draft pick to post a 40-homer season.
Yes, only the second.
Obviously, the Yankees have more than fair share of elite sluggers in history. It's just that many of the homegrown ones entered the league before 1965, when the MLB Draft was first instituted. Others began their careers with other teams before joining the Yankees.
Here is the complete list of Yankees players to post a 40-homer season and how they joined New York, with pre-draft players italicized:
- Aaron Judge (draft pick)
- Roger Maris (trade)
- Mickey Mantle (signed)
- Lou Gehrig (signed)
- Joe DiMaggio (signed)
- Tino Martinez (trade)
- Reggie Jackson (free agent)
- Ben Rice (draft pick)
There are other Yankees draft picks who have come close, with Fred McGriff, Steve Balboni and Don Mattingly all posting a season with at least 35 homers.
McGriff, a ninth-round Yankees pick in 1981, came closest to 40 among that group with 37 in a 1993 season split between the Atlanta Braves and San Diego Padres. He never played a game for New York, having been traded as minor leaguer in a now-infamous deal for Dale Murray and Tom Dodd.
As for some other famous names, Derek Jeter never hit more than 24 and Bernie Williams never hit more than 30.
It's all a fun little quirk of history, created by the flow of both the Yankees and the MLB rulebook through the time. It actually requires quite a lot to go right for a draft pick to hit 40 homers in even a single season.

- SNL experiments with putting basketball, football, and other sports stars at the center of comedy.
Jalen Brunson’s victory lap is apparently still going. After leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship in 53 years and earning Finals MVP honors, the point guard will trade Madison Square Garden for Studio 8H when he hosts the Season 52 premiere of Saturday Night Live on September 26, 2026. KATSEYE will make its SNL debut as the music guest.
It’ll be Brunson’s first time hosting, and he’ll become the first Knicks player ever to host the show. He’s also the first active NBA player to get the gig since LeBron James opened Season 33 in 2007. Brunson has already been getting increasingly comfortable in the entertainment world — he recently popped up during the Emmys and filmed a guest appearance for Law & Order: SVU — though he joked ahead of SNL that he’s “probably not” prepared for whatever the writers are about to throw at him.
That uncertainty is part of what makes athletes on SNL so interesting. We normally see them in tightly controlled press conferences, commercials or postgame interviews, but sketch comedy requires them to loosen up, laugh at themselves and occasionally look completely ridiculous on live television. Since quarterback Fran Tarkenton became the first pro athlete to host in 1977, everyone from NBA legends and Super Bowl champions to tennis stars, Olympians and baseball players has stepped onto the SNL stage. Brunson will soon get his turn. Until then, here are some of the most memorable athletes who have hosted Saturday Night Live.
Michael Jordan (1991)
Fresh off his first NBA championship, Jordan hosted the Season 17 premiere on September 28, 1991, with Public Enemy serving as musical guest. His appearance in the Chicago-centric “Bill Swerski’s Super Fans” was practically inevitable, but his wonderfully straight-faced session with Al Franken’s Stuart Smalley in “Daily Affirmation” remains one of the best examples of SNL figuring out exactly how to use a superstar athlete.
Peyton Manning (2007)
Manning arrived at SNL only weeks after winning Super Bowl XLI and immediately proved he was willing to go all-in on the joke. His infamous United Way digital short flipped his wholesome quarterback image on its head by depicting him as an absolutely terrible influence on a group of children, and the sketch has remained tied to Manning’s comedy résumé ever since.
O.J. Simpson (1978)
Decades before the murder trial that would completely reshape his public image, Simpson hosted SNL on February 25, 1978, with Ashford & Simpson as musical guests. The episode included Simpson delivering his monologue as a Conehead and spoofing the famous Hertz commercials that had helped make him one of the most recognizable athlete endorsers in America.
Bill Russell (1979)
Russell became one of the earliest sports legends to host SNL when he took over Studio 8H on November 3, 1979, with Chicago as the musical guest. The NBA icon appeared throughout an episode that included “Sports Hotline,” “The Black Shadow,” and a Barry White-themed sketch, making Russell one of the show’s earliest experiments with putting a basketball superstar at the center of a comedy show.
Travis Kelce (2023)
Kelce was already known as one of the NFL’s biggest personalities before hosting in March 2023, but SNL gave him a chance to show that his charisma could translate outside of football. His episode leaned into everything from his reputation as an overly enthusiastic bro to the inherent comedy of seeing a 6-foot-5 NFL right end dropped into increasingly bizarre situations, helping kickstart an even bigger run for him in mainstream entertainment.
Charles Barkley (1993, 2010, 2012 & 2018)
Nobody on this list embraced SNL quite like Charles Barkley. Sir Charles has hosted four times, beginning with the 1993 season premiere alongside Nirvana and returning in 2010, 2012 and 2018, long after his playing career ended. His willingness to make fun of himself — and the same unfiltered personality that eventually made him a television star — made him unusually well suited for the format.
Derek Jeter (2001)
Yankees captain Derek Jeter hosted on December 1, 2001, at the height of his New York celebrity, with Shakira and Bubba Sparxxx appearing as music guests. Naturally, SNL went heavy on baseball, most memorably putting Jeter in drag as one of the “Baseball Wives” sitting in the Yankee Stadium stands alongside Rachel Dratch, Amy Poehler, Maya Rudolph and Ana Gasteyer.
Chris Evert (1989)
Tennis legend Chris Evert became one of the relatively few women athletes to host the show when she took the stage on November 11, 1989. Her episode immediately poked fun at her famously composed demeanor, opening with a sketch imagining Evert completely losing it after a Wimbledon defeat before she used her monologue to compare the pressure of live television to playing professional tennis.
Ronda Rousey (2016)
Rousey hosted in January 2016, only a few months after Holly Holm handed her the first loss of her MMA career. She addressed that defeat during her monologue before jumping into sketches including “Bland Man,” “Teacher’s Trial,” and a bit alongside Cecily Strong and musical guest Selena Gomez. The appearance came at an interesting moment in Rousey’s career, as she was beginning to move more heavily into movies, television and eventually professional wrestling.
Deion Sanders (1995)
There may never have been a host better suited to the phrase “Prime Time.” Sanders hosted in February 1995 while still famously balancing careers in the NFL and Major League Baseball, and SNL naturally leaned into his outsized personality with sketches about the baseball strike and the ESPYs. He even performed his own songs, “Must Be The Money” and “It’s On,” during the episode while Bon Jovi handled the official musical guest duties.
LeBron James (2007)
Just a few months after leading Cleveland to his first NBA Finals, a 22-year-old LeBron James hosted the Season 33 premiere on September 29, 2007. Kanye West was the musical guest, while James showed a playful side of himself in sketches that included Kristen Wiig’s increasingly absurd Penelope character and jokes about what his family was supposedly doing while he was busy hosting the show.
Wayne Gretzky (1989)
“The Great One” became the first hockey player to host SNL when he appeared on May 13, 1989, alongside musical guest Fine Young Cannibals. The writers unsurprisingly built plenty of material around hockey — including “Stanley Cup Loss” and “Wakiki Hockey” — while Gretzky also stepped into one of that era’s signature recurring sketches, “Wayne’s World.”

The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees fans are frustrated. It's been 17 long years since they've enjoyed a parade down the Canyon of Heroes following a World Series victory. The man primarily responsible for that frustration is general manager Brian Cashman.
If you ask veteran MLB insider Ken Rosenthal, though, Cashman is doing a bang-up job. Rosenthal gushed about Cashman during a recent appearance on Foul Territory.
"It's time, it's past time, to understand what [Brian] Cashman has accomplished," Rosenthal said. "And all of those years finishing above .500, since 1998, yes, they have had financial advantages, too. So have a lot of other teams. No other team has had a winning record every year.
"Now I know, certain fans, certain Yankees fans, will say, 'No World Series title since 2009.' Yes, that is true. It's undeniable, and some of the teams have not been constructed as well as they could've been. I would expect Cashman would say that as well. However, they are always in the mix."
He went on to acknowledge what the standard is in New York - World Series or bust - and he detailed that through line from George Steinbrenner to Derek Jeter to Aaron Judge. But ultimately, his point was that the playoffs are random and that Cashman shouldn't be held accountable for not winning a ring since 2009. Regular season greatness, in Rosenthal's opinion, is a better measuring stick of a GM's abilities.
Sounds ridiculous, right? Even if we grant him that the World Series is tough to win, and it is, that's the point! We're still looking at a clear decline. Think back to the dynasty that began in 1996. The Yankees won four World Series, yes, but they had also lost two others (2001, 2003), meaning that during an eight-year stretch they made it to the final showdown six times. Now consider that since 2009 they only have one World Series appearance to their credit: the 2024 defeat at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
It's hard not to see a distinct break. Remember, too, that Cashman ascended to the role of general manager on February 3, 1998. He's not fully responsible for those championship clubs, as they had been molded and shaped by Gene Michael and Bob Watson before him.
Also remember that during the 2008-2009 offseason, Cashman's seat was scorching hot, and he was basically mandated by George to go on the huge spending spree that netted New York CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira, and A.J. Burnett. If his hand hadn't been forced, we likely wouldn't have seen those splashes, and we don't have the ring to show for it.
An honest assessment of Brian Cashman's Yankees tenure pegs him as a middle-of-the-pack general manager
Going back to Rosenthal for a second, he's also been on an apology tour for Cincinnati Reds president of baseball operations, Nick Krall. Krall runs a small-market team, but he enjoys having an MVP-caliber player in Elly De La Cruz, a young ace in Chase Burns, and the likely NL Rookie of the Year in Sal Stewart on pre-arb contracts. That trio makes up just under $2.5 million of Cincinnati's $133 million payroll. He could've set the remaining $130 million on fire and gotten better results.
I bring this up as a reminder that insiders like Rosenthal's sole job is to get inside information and break stories. They get that by cultivating relationships, so when you hear them give an edgy or unconventional opinion, it's because they don't want to hurt a source's feelings.
This isn't to say that Cashman is a bad GM. He's made his share of great moves. He's made blockbuster trades like acquiring Alex Rodriguez, Giancarlo Stanton, and Juan Soto. He's found diamonds in the rough like Brent Headrick (and several others).
But the issue with Cashman is that he doesn't learn from his past mistakes. After failing to acquire prime Johan Santana to protect Phil Hughes, Joba Chamberlain, and Ian Kennedy, he let Ivan Nova, Eduardo Nunez, and Adam Warren stand in the way of trading for Cliff Lee a few years later. Then he compounded the mistake when he failed to sign Lee the following offseason.
In recent years, he's failed to capitalize on Aaron Judge being the literal reincarnation of Babe Ruth by shying away from emptying out the farm to acquire difference makers who would have changed the Yankees' calculus.
It's impossible to look at his missteps and not see titles left on the table. It's criminal that he's enjoyed the best hitter this generation has produced, yet since 2017 has just one World Series appearance to show for it.
Go back to the 1998 team. That should have been his lesson. That club laid waste to the American League, winning 114 games. Entering October, a World Series berth felt inevitable. Going into the World Series against the San Diego Padres, the only question was whether the Yankees would hoist the Commissioner's Trophy after four games or five.
Since those glory days, winning the division is no longer a guarantee. Making the playoffs has sometimes felt like it's on shaky ground. The standard has been lowered, but by the organization, not the fans.

item.content:encoded:
MOOSIC — Edinson Duran became the unlikely answer to a trivia question.
Sunday’s season finale between the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders and Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp at PNC Field was canceled due to rain and wet grounds. That meant Saturday night’s game was the last one featuring the RailRiders nickname. The team is rebranding and expected to announce the new identity in November.
So when people ask who was the winning pitcher in the final game of the RailRiders era, it isn’t a top prospect like Elmer Rodriguez or an ace like Brendan Beck. It is Duran, a catcher who spent more time on the development list this season than the active roster.
Whenever the RailRiders would need to use a position player to save arms in the bullpen, they would go to Duran. He’s done it eight times in the past two seasons, including six this season.
In the top of the 10th inning Saturday night, Justin Topa struck out the first two batters with the automatic runner on second base. However, with the count 2-1 to Logan Driscoll, Topa reached his pitch limit. With no other options, manager Shelley Duncan called upon Duran. The 24-year old from Venezuela walked Driscoll, then walked Gage Miller to load the bases, but got Johnny Olmstead to fly out to center fielder Duke Ellis to end the inning. The RailRiders won in the bottom of the 10th, 6-5, when automatic runner Yanquiel Fernandez scored from third base on a wild pitch, making Duran the winning pitcher.
“It was really exciting for Duran to come in and do what he did,” RailRiders reliever Eric Reyzelman said. “It’s fun, kind of reminds you why you play this game. Technically, we had nothing on the line playoff-wise. But we did not want to leave this place without a win.”
And so the RailRiders’ final ride has pulled into the station. The team finished 78-68 overall (37-37 first half, 41-31 second half). Its all-time record wound up 1,028 wins and 834 losses.
From the first pitch by Vidal Nuño to Pawtucket’s Brock Holt on April 4, 2013, to the last one Saturday night — Jacksonville’s Stephen Jones’ wild pitch with Kenedy Corona batting — a lot of memorable moments happened in between.
Six times the RailRiders made the playoffs. Three times they lost in the International League championship series (2017, 2018, 2025). But in 2016, they defeated the Gwinnett Braves in four games to capture the IL title, then beat the Pacific Coast League champion El Paso Chihuahuas to claim the Triple-A national championship.
Many notable players have worn a RailRiders uniform.
Hall of Famer Derek Jeter spent seven games on a rehab assignment in early July 2013 while recovering from a broken ankle. During his time here, it became a daily game to see where he was spotted in downtown Scranton.
Later that month, Alex Rodriguez played three games here while coming back from offseason hip surgery. He hit a two-run home run in the second at-bat of his first game.
Curtis Granderson and D.J. LeMahieu were other notable Yankees who rehabbed here over the years. This season, pitchers Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and outfielder Cody Bellinger had rehab stints.
Current Yankees slugger Aaron Judge played 154 games with the RailRiders in 2015 and 2016 and five more games on a rehab assignment in 2019. He totaled 28 home runs and 95 RBIs. Prospects such as Gary Sanchez, Anthony Volpe and George Lombard Jr. spent time here.
“A lot of great players have played for the RailRiders,” said Beck, who wound up leading the International League in earned-run average (2.93), strikeouts (151), innings (135.1), WHIP (1.06) and opponents’ batting average (.210). “To be the last ones to do it is fun. The future is exciting as well. Looking forward to starting something new next year. But to be the team to end the RailRiders dynasty on a comeback win with a good crowd at home is a lot of fun. Definitely a fun day at the office.”
When Duncan played in Scranton/Wilkes-Barre from 2007-09, the team was known as the Yankees. But in his four seasons as manager, the term “RailRiders” has come to mean a lot to him.
“I just always think about the character of every team that I’ve had,” said Duncan, whose record as RailRiders manager is 327-195. “I’ve been lucky to be a part of some good groups that fought all the way to the end. Some good memories and some good relationships. Each year has been a different team and each year has been very special.”
Clint Frazier was a top prospect who played 213 games for the RailRiders from 2016-19 before a severe concussion and lingering symptoms ultimately sidetracked his career. Because of his frequent shuttling between the minors and the majors, he proclaimed himself a “RailRider for Life.”
He made an appearance at Saturday night’s game, signing autographs for fans and throwing out the ceremonial first pitch.
“It was me being a little facetious,” Frazier said. “I think it started around the time I got optioned to the minor leagues in 2019. I was doing relatively well at the big-league level. When I came down here, there was something in the media about September roster expansion and the Yankees were kind of vague on whether I going to be coming back. I remember parking in a parking garage and seeing this sign that said ‘Scranton Life’ and I was like, ‘Dude, I don’t want to be a Yankee. I want to be a RailRider for Life.’ It was a facetious comment and I ended up running with it because it was kind of funny. People obviously took notice to it because I put it on my Twitter bio and it’s been there for like 10 years.”
Frazier was a little surprised and a bit disappointed when he heard the team was rebranding and retiring the RailRiders nickname.
“I’m not a part of the Yankees anymore and I’m not here in Scranton,” Frazier said. “So if they want to rebrand or it’s something the fans want, you give them it. But other than that, I was kind of like, ‘Damn, I guess I won’t be a RailRider anymore. I’ll be whatever they are.’ But I’ll still be a RailRider at heart.”
The nickname has not only meant something to players.
Kristina Knight has been with the team for 20 seasons. She started as an intern with the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Red Barons, then worked in tickets sales and group sales, sponsor servicing and currently is senior director of partnership management and marketing.
“I think it was extra special because it was a community-thought name,” Knight said. “We surveyed the community and did the poll of submitting your ideas. So I like to think it was the community’s name, which was extra special within itself. The reason we went away from the Yankees name was to give the area more ownership of the team here. I think it did that for sure.
“When we were the Yankees, it was very nice and obviously nice to be included in the Yankees family. But the RailRiders was our very own name and gave our own identity in the minor-league baseball world.”
When the new nickname is announced in November, Knight believes that the community will accept it as well.
“I think it will be as well-received and special to the community,” Knight said. “We are trying to make sure it reflects everything in this area that we find very special and attractive about our area and try to make it a highlight to the nation.”

The New York Yankees aren't nicknamed the Bronx Bombers for no reason. For that reason, they've been well represented in the Louisville Slugger Silver Slugger Awards throughout the years. The Yankees have multiple representatives at every position except for one: shortstop.
This is in part because the award was first introduced in 1980, meaning that franchise greats and champions like Phil Rizzuto and Frank Crosetti missed the boat by a large margin. Another mitigating factor is that New York had one player dominate the position for much of the Silver Slugger era. That, of course, is Derek Jeter, who had a stranglehold on the position for the better part of two decades, taking home the award five times himself.
But while it seems like yesterday, Jeter's last big league season was in 2014. Since then, the position has looked pretty bleak. From 2015 through the present day, the Yankees have gotten a .715 OPS out of the position, which ranks 15th in the majors during that span.
That number includes the Didi Gregorius years, which included some very fine performances. Gregorius hit 97 homers in pinstripes over five seasons, while slashing .269/.313/.446. That's nothing to sneeze at, but he was never the AL's best hitter at the position during his time here.
Gregorius left following the 2019 season, and since then, things have been bleak. From 2020 onward, we have mostly been dealing with Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Anthony Volpe at short. In that time period, Yankees shortstops have produced a .668 OPS, ranking 26th in baseball.
The Yankees can't continue getting subpar offensive production out of the shortstop position
Right now, the hope for the future is George Lombard Jr. The club's top prospect got off to a hot start, but since then, he's cooled substantially. It's too early to write him off just yet, especially at just 21 years old. However, the Yankees can't afford to get into another Volpe-esque holding pattern where years go by and no material improvements are made.
That leaves the front office with an interesting conundrum. Shortstops who can hit and field don't grow on trees, and while Brian Cashman passed on a generational shortstop free-agent class to sign IKF to keep the seat warm for Volpe, he cannot afford to repeat the same lethargic approach to the position.
Ideally, Lombard Jr. snatches the job for the next 20 years with a strong finish to 2026, a postseason to remember, and a spring training that eliminates all doubt. Jeter met with the promising youngster to advise him on the responsibilities that lie ahead. Now we'll see if he took those lessons to heart.
But if we come to the conclusion of New York's 2026 campaign and haven't seen Lombard Jr. show signs that he can consistently rise to the occasion; the Yankees must be opportunistic when it comes to pursuing upgrades.
After being wrapped up in rumors at the trade deadline, it's thought that the Angels could revisit trade talks for Zach Neto in the offseason. Another possible scenario is that the Astros follow the Kyle Tucker path and trade Jeremy Peña this winter ahead of his final year of team control.
In an ideal situation, the Yankees could acquire a player like Neto or Peña while retaining Lombard Jr. to hedge their bets. Worst-case scenario: Lombard Jr. busts, and the team has a high-end veteran to man the position. Best-case scenario: they have to undertake some shuffling, but Lombard Jr. is a star, and the team is deeper and better for it.
What can't happen is the Yankees put all their eggs in the Lombard Jr. bucket, and then miss out on young stars in their prime and let the position languish for another half-decade. The time to wait and see is over, and the time to be bold is now.

item.content:encoded:
Rudy Martin Jr. waited 12 years for an opportunity that lasted three days. And the shame of it is, he never really got to run.
Called up by the Toronto Blue Jays last Friday, Martin was wearing a big league uniform for the first time at age 30. He had been drafted in 2014 and played stints in Mexico and two independent leagues before the Blue Jays decided a guy with 45 stolen bases in 91 minor league games might help them make the MLB playoffs.
Martin pinch-ran last Friday, he played seven innings Saturday, and he went on the injured list with a strained hamstring Monday. He never went first to third, never scored on a sacrifice fly, never attempted to steal second base. There is little guarantee he will ever get another chance.
But 10 years ago, his chances would have been annual events.
Martin was, for one weekend, a throwback to a not-so-distant era when anonymous minor leaguers arrived every September and made big league names for themselves with their speed. Some of those September call-ups eventually established long careers, turning exciting moments as stretch-run pinch-runners into lasting big league paychecks.
Martin might have been one of those annual call-ups, but he did not reach Class AAA until 2019, the year before MLB limited September call-ups to two players per team, effectively condemning September pinch-runners to near extinction, and making it harder for anyone to run so fast that major league teams simply could not ignore them.
"Having speed and chasing the playoffs definitely had a big impact and gave me more opportunities than I would if I did not have this speed," Atlanta Braves first-base coach Antoan Richardson said.
Richardson got to the big leagues twice as a player, each time as a September call-up for a team in contention. He debuted with Atlanta in 2011, then he scored the winning run on Derek Jeter's final Yankee Stadium at-bat in 2014. Jeter's much-replayed walk-off single featured a player with only 20 career at-bats.
Under the old rules, players like Richardson arrived every September. But these days, having one tool is no longer enough for such specialized, game-changing players to get a foot in the door.
"Call-ups in September have changed completely," said Tim Locastro, who ran his way onto a big league roster in 2017.
For decades, September rosters could expand to 40 players. Teams rarely activated that many, but 30-plus was typical, and clubhouses became overcrowded with redundancy and specialization. One-dimensional pinch-runners were not the only September luxury. Third catchers were standard, and top prospects were often promoted despite having little to do but get acclimated to the major leagues -- in 1993, Atlanta called up 21-year-old Chipper Jones and gave him three at-bats.
One major league executive, granted anonymity to speak candidly, noted that the widespread youth and athleticism of modern rosters could be a contributing factor in the decline of September runners -- teams do not necessarily need to pinch-run as often -- but said that the 28-man roster limit was surely the main reason so few teams seem interested in finding the next Terrance Gore.
Last year's Los Angeles Dodgers carried Justin Dean as a dedicated late-season pinch-runner and defensive replacement, but the Dodgers, with their unusual depth, are outliers. Few other teams feel they can devote a roster spot to such a limited player.
There was a brief attempt, a half-century ago, to make pinch-running a season-long occupation. The Oakland Athletics of the 1960s and 1970s regularly gave roster spots to players whose main job, or only job, was to pinch-run. Allan Lewis, Don Hopkins, Matt Alexander and Larry Lintz rarely did much else for the A's, but they did a lot of running, and their teams did a lot of winning. Most famous of the team's runners was Herb Washington, an international track star with a minimal baseball background who never hit or played the field but got into 92 games and stole 29 bases in 1974 as the A's won their third consecutive World Series.
Despite the A's success, their designated runner strategy did not catch on, and even the team's owner, Charlie Finley, seemed to lose interest in the idea (though the Pittsburgh Pirates did sign Alexander and use him in much the same way on the way to their own championship in 1979). September roster expansion, though, allowed the concept to survive as an annual, one-month-only tradition.
September call-ups in the 1980s and 1990s often included running specialists -- from Jeff Stone with the Philadelphia Phillies in 1983 to Eddie Miller for the San Diego Padres in 1984 -- but the practice spiked with the data-driven strategy of the 2000s. In 2009, 13 players stole at least 30 bases in Class AAA, and 12 of them were on major league rosters come September. Only one of the dozen had previously spent more than a couple of weeks in the big leagues. Class AAA leaderboards at that time were always littered with September call-ups.
In 2013, the Cincinnati Reds used September expansion to call up 22-year-old Billy Hamilton, who promptly stole 13 bases in 13 games to help the Reds clinch the final wild-card spot in the National League. Two years later, the Atlanta Braves gave a September call-up to 31-year-old Emilio Bonifácio, whom they had designated for assignment just two months earlier. In 2017, Locastro made his major league debut in September and got his first of 29 consecutive stolen bases without being caught, an MLB record for the start of a career.
"That year I got called up in 2017, all August in the minor leagues, I'm trying to show my speed off more than anything," Locastro said. "I knew if I was going to be called up, it was going to be to run the bases."
Some had memorable names -- Esix Snead, Rico Noel, Charlton Jimerson -- but few had notable careers beyond the fact that in the right moment, they could bring a stadium to its feet. Yet the nature of their jobs made them unforgettable to every fan base that got to see them run.
Most famous of the September runners was Gore, who got to the big leagues every year from 2014 to 2022, won three World Series rings with three organizations and became such a Kansas City Royals icon that his death in February prompted online tributes and an opening day ceremony. Gore started only 14 major league games in his career. But he played in 123, including 11 in the postseason; more than half of Gore's appearances came in September, and his only big league action in 2021 was as an Atlanta pinch-runner in a division series. Baseball Reference considers Gore to have 0.1 wins above replacement, but he stole 43 bases, and most of them came off the bench, late in the year, for playoff-bound teams.
"There have been very few players who can take over a baseball game," Dayton Moore, a former Royals general manager, said after Gore died. "That's exactly what he did."
The Class AAA steals leaders this year, Braiden Ward and Duke Ellis, are experienced outfielders in the Red Sox and Yankees farm systems, each with 50-plus steals and their parent clubs in contention.
That was a reliable call-up formula a decade ago, but neither has been promoted. To get Martin on the roster last week, the Blue Jays had to designate for assignment an underperforming veteran, Jesus Sanchez. The call-up was not as simple as putting Martin on the 40-man roster and stitching his name onto a jersey.
Nearly a decade after the September call-up that started his own big league career, Locastro now works as a minor league instructor with the Padres, and part of his job is to teach young players to run the bases. But he has to warn them: Running cannot be all they do.
"Nowadays," Locastro said, "you need to have all aspects of the game if you want to be called up in September."
